lineage_context.teaching_goal: Learn the Caryophyllales family split by comparing tiny papery bracteate flowers and utricle-type fruit against ocreae, anthocarps, and many-seeded capsules.

project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first recognition module across ten project-pool genera
project_scope.note: Project taxonomy follows broad Amaranthaceae including former Chenopodiaceae. Older field guides may still place Atriplex and Chenopodium in Chenopodiaceae.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with the tiny flowers and their papery bracts/bracteoles. Amaranthaceae usually has a single perianth whorl of tepals rather than a distinct calyx + corolla, a superior one-celled ovary, and commonly one ovule/one seed.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Mostly herbs or shrubs; leaves simple, alternate or opposite, without stipules. Some are mealy, succulent, spiny, or salt-adapted.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers small, bisexual or unisexual, commonly crowded into spikes, heads, glomerules or panicles. Bracts and bracteoles are often conspicuous, papery or spine-tipped. Tepals usually 2–5 and persistent.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Often a utricle or achene-like one-seeded fruit; some open circumscissile like a tiny lid, while others remain indehiscent. Persistent tepals/bracts often remain around the fruit.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: LOOK HERE FIRST: isolate ONE flower from a head/spike. Identify the subtending bract, any paired bracteoles, the usually 2–5 persistent tepals (one perianth whorl), then the superior single-chambered ovary and usually one-seeded utricle. Broad Amaranthaceae includes former Chenopodiaceae; Atriplex female flowers may lack an ordinary perianth and are enclosed by enlarged paired bracteoles. Neither one-seeded fruit nor papery heads alone proves the family.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: tiny flower package → persistent tepals/bracts → one-seeded fruit → genus doors → Caryophyllales comparison
visual_lesson.intro: Amaranthaceae is easier when you zoom in. What looks like a fuzzy spike is a stack of tiny flowers, papery bracts and persistent tepals surrounding a one-seeded fruit.

steps.title: 1 · Zoom into the papery flower package
steps.look_for: Very small flowers packed into heads/spikes, each with persistent tepals and usually papery bracts or bracteoles.
steps.why_it_matters: This separates the family from Caryophyllaceae's more obvious petals and Polygonaceae's ocrea-first architecture.

steps.title: 2 · Follow one flower to one seed
steps.look_for: A tiny fruit enclosing one seed; in some Amaranthus the top comes off circumscissile like a lid.
steps.why_it_matters: The one-seeded fruit is a powerful family-level reproductive clue.

steps.title: 3 · Amaranthus door: bristly spikes and utricles
steps.look_for: Crowded greenish flower clusters, often with sharp bracts; fruit commonly a utricle that may split around the middle.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the most familiar amaranth architecture and makes a useful family anchor.

steps.title: 4 · Alternanthera/Gomphrena door: white papery heads
steps.look_for: Opposite leaves and white/straw-colored papery heads or spikes; Alternanthera has pseudostaminodes alternating with fertile stamens.
steps.why_it_matters: These genera show how showy 'flowers' can mostly be persistent papery floral parts.

steps.title: 5 · Atriplex/Chenopodium door: former goosefoots
steps.look_for: Often gray-green or mealy foliage and very reduced greenish flowers. In Atriplex, female fruits are often enclosed by paired enlarging bracteoles.
steps.why_it_matters: This explicitly connects older Chenopodiaceae field-guide concepts to modern broad Amaranthaceae.

steps.title: 6 · Froelichia/Iresine/Tidestromia doors
steps.photo_role: woolly spike / open panicle / hairy glomerule
steps.look_for: Froelichia makes woolly spikes with hardened fruiting perianths; Iresine can form open panicles and be dioecious; Tidestromia has dense branched/barbed hairs and axillary glomerules.
steps.why_it_matters: The family contains several very different silhouettes that become understandable once the tiny flower/fruit plan is known.

comparisons.title: Amaranthaceae vs Caryophyllaceae
comparisons.rule: Compare an isolated flower and fruit: Amaranthaceae commonly has one whorl of persistent tepals, bracts/bracteoles and a single-loculed, usually one-seeded utricle. Many Caryophyllaceae have separate sepals and petals plus a many-seeded capsule, BUT Paronychia can be apetalous and one-seeded. Confirm floral parts, not seed count alone.

comparisons.title: Amaranthaceae vs Polygonaceae
comparisons.rule: Inspect a leaf node and an isolated fruit: many Polygonaceae have an ocrea (stipular sheath) and a 2–3-angled achene; Eriogonum is a crucial no-ocrea exception, recognized with involucral flower clusters. Amaranthaceae lacks an ocrea and usually presents bracteate flowers with persistent tepals around a one-seeded utricle.

comparisons.title: Amaranthaceae vs Nyctaginaceae
comparisons.rule: Dissect the fruiting flower: Nyctaginaceae develops a persistent, perianth-derived anthocarp enclosing the true one-seeded fruit (e.g., Mirabilis), whereas Amaranthaceae commonly has distinct bract/bracteole and tepal layers surrounding a utricle. Both may be small-flowered and one-seeded; a showy tube is not required in Nyctaginaceae.

comparisons.title: Amaranthaceae vs Euphorbiaceae (Acalypha)
comparisons.rule: Acalypha pistillate bracts can resemble pigweed bracts, but its superior ovary/capsule is usually three-carpellate and three-locular, often splitting into three one-seeded segments. Typical Amaranthus has a one-loculed utricle containing one seed. Compare dissected ovaries/fruits, not the cluster silhouette.

visual_lesson.caveat: Broad Amaranthaceae is diverse and includes former Chenopodiaceae. Circumscissile fruit, mealy foliage, spines, and opposite leaves are genus-level clues, not family-wide requirements.

family_confusion_polish.look_here_first: Take one flower and one ripe fruit from the cluster: bract below, paired bracteoles if present, tepals around a superior one-loculed ovary, and the usually single seed. Identify these layers individually before naming the family.
exceptions: Atriplex pistillate flowers often lack a conventional perianth; the two enlarged fruiting bracteoles are not petals or tepals.
Paronychia (Caryophyllaceae) can lack petals and have one-seeded fruit, defeating the shortcut 'one seed = Amaranthaceae'.
Eriogonum (Polygonaceae) lacks the obvious ocrea seen in many other Polygonaceae; examine involucral cups and individual achenes.
Circumscissile opening, mealiness, spines, papery heads and opposite leaves are not universal Amaranthaceae characters.
genus_routing: Amaranthus: spike/glomerule + bract/tepal/utricle; A. spinosus has paired nodal spines; A. palmeri often has separate male and female plants.
Atriplex: paired enlarging pistillate bracteoles; do not demand a conventional perianth.
Chenopodium and Monolepis: reduced goosefoot-type flowers; confirm single flower/fruit anatomy.
Alternanthera: opposite leaves and scarious clusters; check fertile stamens versus pseudostaminodes.
Gomphrena and Celosia: individual papery flowers within heads or spikes; dissection required.
Froelichia: hardened woolly fruiting perianth; Iresine: often open panicles and separate sexes; Tidestromia: axillary glomerules and branched hairs.
